subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Debt and Cognitive Load
description: A micro-lesson that makes Debt and Cognitive Load usable.

hook.text: People in debt score 13 IQ points lower on cognitive tests. Not because they're less smart.

buildup.text: Mullainathan and Shafir's scarcity research showed that financial stress occupies working memory, leaving less.

discovery.text: Debt creates a tax on thinking. Every decision is filtered through 'can I afford this?' draining energy from everything.

twist.text: This creates a vicious cycle: debt impairs decision-making, which leads to worse financial choices, which creates more.

climax.text: Reducing debt doesn't just save money. It frees mental capacity for better decisions across every domain of life.

punchline.text: Debt doesn't just cost money. It costs thinking.

quiz.question: How does debt affect cognitive performance?
options: It has no effect on thinking
It occupies working memory, reducing capacity for other decisions
It makes people permanently less intelligent

details.summary: Carrying debt consumes mental bandwidth by creating constant background worry about repayment, interest accumulation, and financial vulnerability. This cognitive load reduces the brain's capacity for other decisions, creating a cycle where debt impairs the thinking needed to escape it.
details.whyItMatters: Debt is not just a financial problem but a cognitive one. People in debt make worse decisions across all domains because their mental resources are consumed by financial worry, explaining why poverty traps are so persistent.
takeaways: Debt creates persistent cognitive load that reduces decision-making quality
Financial worry consumes mental bandwidth needed for other life decisions
Debt relief improves cognitive function and decision making beyond finances

faq.question: How does debt affect thinking beyond financial decisions?
faq.answer: Studies show indebted individuals perform worse on cognitive tests, make more impulsive decisions, and have reduced executive function. The mental resources consumed by financial worry leave less capacity for work performance, parenting, and health decisions.

faq.question: Does the type of debt matter for cognitive load?
faq.answer: Yes. High-interest credit card debt creates more cognitive load than a predictable mortgage because its variable nature demands constant monitoring. Multiple small debts are more draining than one larger debt because each is a separate worry.
